The underlying PISA design is a complex, stratified sampling of schools and students, and OECD reporting typically uses sampling weights to produce population-representative estimates and associated uncertainty (e.g., 95% confidence intervals). The factsheet does not specify the exact weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures, so the specific implementation details are not recoverable from the provided text. For any re-analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights as documented in the PISA technical documentation to correctly account for clustering and sampling variability.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in North Macedonia performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how results changed relative to earlier PISA cycles (notably 2015 and 2018). It reports mean performance trends, proficiency-level distributions (e.g., Level 2 baseline and Level 5/6 top performers), and gaps by socio-economic status (ESCS international quintiles and top/bottom 25% groups) and by gender. The assessment uses two two-hour subject tests with different students receiving different combinations of test questions, plus student and school questionnaires; the factsheet also notes that creative thinking was an innovative area and that financial literacy was optional. For North Macedonia, the factsheet reports 6,610 students in 111 schools and indicates that all data met PISA quality standards for reporting. Uncertainty is communicated via 95% confidence intervals, and the note flags that some countries/economies may require caution due to unmet sampling standards (North Macedonia is not flagged).
